periods.activity_title: What Is a Perimeter? Boundary Sums for Rectangles and Squares

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (lace around tablecloth), section 6.1 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Akshi wants to put lace all around a rectangular tablecloth 3 m long and 2 m wide; find the length of lace required using P = 2 × (l + b) = 10 m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Usha runs three rounds), section 6.1 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Usha travels if she takes three rounds of a square park of side 75 m; perimeter = 300 m, total distance = 900 m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm and breadth is 2 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the side length of a square whose perimeter is 20 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 12 m and length is 3 m.

time_bands.activity: Open with a concrete question: ask students how much ribbon is needed to go all the way around a rectangular card. Students trace the boundary with a finger, counting sides. Establish that perimeter is the total boundary distance — the sum of all side lengths — and that opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so the four-side sum collapses to 2 × (l + b).

Walk through Example (lace around tablecloth), section 6.1 p.131 ("Akshi wants to put lace all around a rectangular tablecloth....") and Example (Usha runs three rounds), section 6.1 p.131 ("Find the total distance Usha travels if she takes three rounds...."). For the square park example, invite students to first guess the formula for a square's perimeter before confirming P = 4 × side.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm...."), Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find the side length of a square whose perimeter is 20 cm...."), and Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find missing breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 12 m....") in pairs, working backwards from the perimeter formula to find the unknown dimension.

Pairs share answers; the teacher collects and records the three formulas — rectangle, square, triangle — on the board as a reference students copy. Close with a quick oral check: the teacher names a shape and students call out the formula.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes write P = l × b (confusing perimeter with area) — emphasise boundary vs. region by having them physically trace the edge of a book. The worked examples move from rectangle to square; encourage students to see the square formula as a special case of the rectangle formula where l = b.

periods.activity_title: Triangle Perimeters and Regular Polygon Generalisations

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A wire bent into a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle is straightened and re-bent into a square; find the side length of the square.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third side of a triangle with perimeter 55 cm and two sides 20 cm and 14 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5a, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 36 cm string is formed into a square; find the side length.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5b, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 36 cm string is formed into an equilateral triangle; find the side length.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5c, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 36 cm string is formed into a regular hexagon; find the side length.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.1 p.132
homework.description: Find the cost of fencing a rectangular park 150 m × 120 m at ₹40 per metre.

time_bands.activity: Pose this discovery prompt: 'A piece of wire forms a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle. If I straighten it and rebend it into a square, what is the side?' Students think individually and share. This is Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.132 ("A wire bent into a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle...."). Establish that the perimeter (total wire length) stays constant regardless of shape — a key insight.

Work through the triangle perimeter: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find the third side of a triangle with perimeter 55 cm...."). Then introduce regular polygons — closed figures with all sides equal and all angles equal. Students discover the general rule: perimeter = number of sides × side length. Use this to solve Figure it Out Q5a–c, section 6.1 p.132 ("A 36 cm string is formed into a square/equilateral triangle/regular hexagon....") for the square, equilateral triangle, and regular hexagon.

Students work in small groups on the three string problems, recording their working. Each group explains how dividing the total string length by the number of sides gives the side length. Invite one group to generalise: for any regular n-gon, side = total perimeter ÷ n.
Whole-class discussion: what makes a polygon 'regular'? Students propose their own examples of regular and irregular polygons. Close by writing the general formula on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who divide by the wrong number of sides for the hexagon — a quick reminder that a hexagon has six sides, not four, is enough. Having established that perimeter is the sum of all sides and that a regular polygon's perimeter equals number-of-sides × side-length, the general principle is now in place for comparison problems.
materials: String or thick thread (36 cm lengths, one per group)

periods.activity_title: Concentric Tracks and Positional Reasoning on Rectangular Paths

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Akshi covers in 5 rounds of the outer rectangular track (70 m × 40 m).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Toshi covers in 7 rounds of the inner rectangular track (60 m × 30 m); determine who ran further.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3a-f, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark positions A, B, C on Akshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m; mark X, Y, Z on Toshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.1 p.132
homework.description: A rectangular field 230 m × 160 m is fenced with 3 rounds of rope; find the total rope length needed.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Matha Pachchi scenario with a sketch on the board: two concentric rectangular tracks, outer 70 m × 40 m and inner 60 m × 30 m. Ask: 'Who runs further — Akshi on the outer track or Toshi on the inner?' Students estimate before computing.

Students compute Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.133 ("Find the total distance Akshi covers in 5 rounds of the outer rectangular track....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.133 ("Find the total distance Toshi covers in 7 rounds...."). They compare the totals and justify their reasoning in a sentence.

Students tackle the positional problem: Figure it Out Q3a-f, section 6.1 p.133 ("Mark positions A, B, C on Akshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m...."). They must think about where on the track those cumulative distances land. Encourage students to divide total distance by perimeter to find full rounds completed and then locate the remainder on the track.
Quick debrief: which position problems were hardest and why? Establish the strategy — complete rounds give no net displacement; only the remainder matters for position.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is to mark positions by counting from the wrong corner or going in the wrong direction — insist students agree on a starting corner and direction before they begin. Having established the perimeter formulas, this unit extends them to multi-lap and positional reasoning, which is the richer application the section builds toward.
materials: Whiteboard with a diagram of the two tracks

periods.activity_title: Measuring Irregular Shapes and Straight vs Diagonal Units on Dot Grids

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Estimate and Verify, section 6.1 p.134
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut irregular paper shapes from a rough sheet; estimate total boundary length by eye, then measure with a scale or measuring tape to verify the perimeter. Also discuss whether the perimeter of a dot-grid triangle is 9 straight units or more than 9 units (diagonal vs. straight length).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (straight and diagonal units), section 6.1 p.135
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the perimeters of four dot-grid figures in terms of straight (s) and diagonal (d) units.

time_bands.activity: Each student tears or cuts an irregular shape from a rough sheet and makes a quick eye estimate of how long its boundary is. No measuring yet — just guess and record the number.

Students carry out Estimate and Verify, section 6.1 p.134 ("Cut irregular paper shapes from a rough sheet; estimate total boundary length...."). They measure with a ruler or measuring tape, compare their estimate with the actual value, and discuss why estimation was hard for jagged versus smooth edges.

Move to dot-grid figures: teacher draws a triangle on a dot grid and asks whether the perimeter is simply 9 straight units. Students realise diagonal segments are longer than straight segments and cannot be counted as equal. Students then complete Figure it Out (straight and diagonal units), section 6.1 p.135 ("Write the perimeters of four dot-grid figures in terms of straight (s) and diagonal (d) units."), expressing each perimeter as a combination of s and d.

Class discussion: can we find the exact numerical perimeter from just s and d? Establish that without the actual length of d we can only express, not compute, the perimeter. Students note the distinction between exact and approximate measurement.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume all grid segments are equal — the diagonal-vs-straight discussion is a genuine conceptual surprise and worth dwelling on. Watch for students who count vertices rather than sides when tracing the boundary of irregular shapes.

periods.activity_title: Split and Rejoin — How Reconfiguring a Rectangle Changes Its Boundary

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular paper chit into two equal halves and rejoin in four different configurations (a–d); find the perimeter of each arrangement and then find an arrangement with perimeter 22 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q b, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement b (two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces joined in an L-shape with 2 cm overlap).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q c, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement c (two pieces joined in a T-shape).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q d, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement d (two pieces joined in a staircase configuration).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin (target 22 cm), section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange the two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces to form a figure with perimeter exactly 22 cm.

time_bands.activity: Each student cuts or is given a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular strip and cuts it into two equal 6 cm × 2 cm halves. Ask: 'What is the perimeter of the original rectangle?' (20 cm). 'Will every rejoined arrangement have the same perimeter?' Students predict yes or no and justify.

Students carry out Split and rejoin, section 6.1 p.136 ("Cut a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular paper chit into two equal halves...."), forming arrangements b, c, and d. They measure or compute the perimeter of each: Split and rejoin Q b, section 6.1 p.136 ("Find the perimeter of arrangement b...."), Split and rejoin Q c, section 6.1 p.136 ("Find the perimeter of arrangement c...."), Split and rejoin Q d, section 6.1 p.136 ("Find the perimeter of arrangement d....").

Challenge: using the two halves, find an arrangement whose perimeter is exactly 22 cm — Split and rejoin (target 22 cm), section 6.1 p.136 ("Arrange the two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces to form a figure with perimeter exactly 22 cm."). Students experiment and justify why their arrangement achieves that total.
Class consolidation: how does the number of shared edges between the two pieces affect the perimeter? Establish the key idea — each centimetre of shared edge removes 2 cm from the perimeter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently forget to subtract the two hidden edges at the join — prompt them to trace the outer boundary only. The critical insight that each shared side reduces the perimeter by twice its length is worth making explicit before moving on.
materials: Pre-cut or student-cut 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular strips

periods.activity_title: Nine-Square Arrangements — Exploring the Range of Achievable Perimeters

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less', section 6.1 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange or draw different connected figures made from 9 unit squares; find the smallest and largest possible perimeters, make a figure with perimeter 18 units, and explore the effect of attaching one more unit square to a figure of perimeter 24 units.

time_bands.activity: Each student draws or arranges 9 unit squares in a connected figure on grid paper. Collect a quick sample of different arrangements from around the class. Ask: 'Do all arrangements have the same perimeter?' Students measure one arrangement each and share.

Students systematically explore Making it 'More' or 'Less', section 6.1 p.145 ("Arrange or draw different connected figures made from 9 unit squares...."), seeking the smallest possible perimeter — the compact 3 × 3 square arrangement giving 12 units — and the largest — the linear 1 × 9 strip giving 20 units. They record each attempt and reason about why compact shapes have smaller perimeters.

Challenge: make a connected arrangement of 9 unit squares with perimeter exactly 18 units. Then explore: if a figure of 9 squares has perimeter 24 units and one more square is attached, what perimeters are possible? Students reason about whether attaching a square by one, two, or three sides changes the count differently.
Class summary: record all discovered perimeters on the board. Are all even-number perimeters between 12 and 20 achievable? Establish the general reasoning about shared sides.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is drawing disconnected figures — insist that every square must share at least one full side with another. Students may need prompting to see that attaching by two sides removes more perimeter than attaching by one side.

periods.activity_title: Area Formulas for Rectangles and Squares — Direct and Composite Problems

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (floor and carpet), section 6.2 p.137
textbook_items_in_class.description: A floor 5 m × 4 m has a square carpet of side 3 m laid on it; find the area of the floor that is not carpeted: 20 – 9 = 11 sq m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (four flower beds), section 6.2 p.137-138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A piece of land 12 m × 10 m has four square flower beds of side 4 m at the four corners; find the area of the remaining part: 120 – 64 = 56 sq m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A rectangular garden 25 m long has area 300 sq m; find the width.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the cost of tiling a 500 m × 200 m plot at ₹8 per 100 sq m.

time_bands.activity: Start with a concrete build-up: draw a 3 × 4 grid on the board and count the squares by rows (4 per row × 3 rows = 12). Generalise: area of a rectangle = l × b. For a square, all sides equal, so area = s². Ask students where else they have seen 'square units' — tiling a floor, covering a field — to recall the concept from everyday experience.

Walk through Example (floor and carpet), section 6.2 p.137 ("A floor 5 m × 4 m has a square carpet of side 3 m laid on it....") and Example (four flower beds), section 6.2 p.137-138 ("A piece of land 12 m × 10 m has four square flower beds...."). Emphasise the composite-subtraction method: large area minus small area(s).

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.138 ("A rectangular garden 25 m long has area 300 sq m; find the width.") — working backwards from area to find a dimension — and Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.138 ("Find the cost of tiling a 500 m × 200 m plot at ₹8 per 100 sq m."), which applies area to a costing context.
Quick oral check: teacher gives area and one dimension; students call out the missing dimension. Reinforce the two formulas and the composite-subtraction idea.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly multiply length by length twice instead of length by breadth — a quick reminder that the two dimensions in l × b must be different sides helps. The composite-subtraction technique appears in both worked examples and will recur throughout the section.

periods.activity_title: Area in Context — Coconut Groves, Composite Figures and Splitting into Rectangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A coconut grove 100 m × 50 m; each tree needs 25 sq m; find the maximum number of trees.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4a, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Split figure a (L-shaped composite) into rectangles and find its area in metres.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4b, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Split figure b (rectangular frame) into rectangles and find its area in metres.

time_bands.activity: Pose the coconut-grove question as a puzzle: the grove has a known area; each tree needs a fixed area — how many trees fit? Students work on Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.138 ("A coconut grove 100 m × 50 m; each tree needs 25 sq m....") and see that area division is the core operation.

Students tackle the composite-figure problems. For Figure it Out Q4a, section 6.2 p.138 ("Split figure a (L-shaped composite) into rectangles....") and Figure it Out Q4b, section 6.2 p.138 ("Split figure b (rectangular frame) into rectangles...."), they draw their own splitting lines on the figure and record the sub-areas before summing. Encourage at least two different splits for the L-shape to show that the total area is the same regardless of how the region is divided.

Pairs compare their different splits of the L-shape and confirm the totals agree. Discuss: can we also compute the L-shape by taking a large rectangle and subtracting a corner? Students verify both methods give the same answer.
Summary: two strategies for composite regions — split into parts and add, or take a large enclosing rectangle and subtract. Both are valid; the choice depends on what dimensions are given.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes split a composite figure incorrectly, leaving a gap or overlap — insist they label each sub-rectangle's dimensions before computing. Having established area formulas for basic shapes, this unit extends them to composite and quotient contexts.

periods.activity_title: Tangram Area Comparisons — Reasoning Without Formulas

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using tangram pieces, explore and identify which pieces have the same area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how many times bigger Shape D is compared to Shape C; describe the relationship between Shapes C, D, and E.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape D or Shape F; give reasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape F or Shape G; give reasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare the area of Shape A to Shape G; determine whether A is twice or four times as big as G.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.2 p.139
homework.description: Find the area of the big square formed with all seven tangram pieces in terms of the area of Shape C.

time_bands.activity: Distribute or students draw the seven tangram pieces. Introduce the task: without measuring, which pieces look like they have the same area? Students discuss in pairs using physical or drawn pieces.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.139 ("Using tangram pieces, explore and identify which pieces have the same area."), Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.139 ("Determine how many times bigger Shape D is compared to Shape C...."), Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.139 ("Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape D or Shape F...."), and Figure it Out Q4, section 6.2 p.139 ("Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape F or Shape G...."), reasoning from superposition or decomposition rather than formula.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q5, section 6.2 p.139 ("Compare the area of Shape A to Shape G; determine whether A is twice or four times as big as G."). They justify answers by overlapping pieces or expressing each piece as a multiple of the smallest piece (Shape C).

Class discussion: can the same reasoning chain establish the area of the whole tangram square? Students begin to see that all pieces together equal a fixed multiple of Shape C — a preview of the homework question.

periods.teacher_notes: The tangram activity develops area intuition without calculation — discourage students from measuring and encourage reasoning by superposition or decomposition into halves. A common confusion is treating differently shaped pieces with the same area as having the same perimeter; the opportunity to distinguish the two concepts is valuable here.

periods.activity_title: Why Squares? Tiling Arguments and the Fixed-Area Rectangle Exploration

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange the 7 tangram pieces into a rectangle and state its area in terms of Shape C; give reasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare the perimeters of the square and the rectangle formed from the 7 tangram pieces; explain whether they are the same or different.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore (24 sq units), section 6.2 p.141
textbook_items_in_class.description: On grid paper, make as many whole-number rectangles as possible with area 24 sq units; identify which has the greatest perimeter (a), the least perimeter (b), and explore the pattern for area 32 sq cm (c).

time_bands.activity: Begin with the 'Why squares?' question from the Let's Explore context: can circles tile a flat surface without gaps or overlaps? Students discuss and draw to see they cannot. Establish that squares (and a few other shapes) tile perfectly, which is why area is measured in square units.

Students complete Figure it Out Q7, section 6.2 p.139 ("Arrange the 7 tangram pieces into a rectangle and state its area in terms of Shape C....") and Figure it Out Q8, section 6.2 p.139 ("Compare the perimeters of the square and the rectangle formed from the 7 tangram pieces...."). The key discovery: same area, different perimeter.

Students work on Let's Explore (24 sq units), section 6.2 p.141 ("On grid paper, make as many whole-number rectangles as possible with area 24 sq units...."). They list all factor pairs of 24 and draw each rectangle, then rank them by perimeter to answer which is greatest (a) and which is least (b). They extend to 32 sq cm for part (c).

Class conjecture: which shape has the smallest perimeter for a fixed area? Students articulate: the rectangle closest to a square shape gives the minimum perimeter, while the most elongated gives the maximum.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes list the same rectangle twice (e.g., 1×24 and 24×1) — clarify that orientation does not produce a new rectangle. The discovery that equal-area rectangles have different perimeters directly challenges the common misconception that area and perimeter always go together.

periods.activity_title: Area Estimation on Grid Paper and Partial-Square Conventions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore Q1, section 6.2 p.141
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area in square metres of the floor outside of the school corridor.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore Q2, section 6.2 p.141
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area in square metres occupied by the school playground.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the four conventions for counting partial squares on a grid: squares more than half filled count as 1; squares less than half filled count as 0; squares exactly half filled count as ½; full squares count as 1. Students record these and practice on two quick irregular shapes drawn on the board.

Students apply the conventions to Let's Explore Q1, section 6.2 p.141 ("Find the area in square metres of the floor outside of the school corridor.") and Let's Explore Q2, section 6.2 p.141 ("Find the area in square metres occupied by the school playground."), drawing or using provided floor-plan outlines on grid paper and systematically marking each square.

Pairs compare their counts for the same figure and discuss discrepancies. Teacher highlights that estimation conventions introduce a small error — the finer the grid, the closer the estimate. Students reason about whether a larger or smaller grid gives a better estimate.
Brief consolidation: area estimation is useful when a figure has curved or irregular edges that cannot be captured by a rectangle formula alone.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often apply partial-square rules inconsistently — suggest they colour full squares in one colour and mark half-squares with a dot to keep the count organised. This unit is a practical application of area measurement that bridges formula-based and estimation-based approaches.
materials: Grid paper with floor-plan outlines (or student-drawn)

periods.activity_title: House Floor Plans — Recovering Missing Dimensions and Computing Total Area

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Charan's house), section 6.2 p.146
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Charan's house floor plan (30 ft × 35 ft overall), find the missing room dimensions and total house area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Sharan's house), section 6.2 p.147
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Sharan's house floor plan (42 ft wide), find missing room dimensions and total area; compare areas and perimeters of both houses.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the house-plan context: a floor plan is a composite of rectangles, with some dimensions given and some to be recovered from the structure. Ask students how they would find a missing room width if they know the overall width and one other room's width.

Students work on Figure it Out (Charan's house), section 6.2 p.146 ("Using Charan's house floor plan (30 ft × 35 ft overall), find the missing room dimensions and total house area."). They label each sub-rectangle, recover missing dimensions using the given overall dimensions, and compute the total area by summing sub-room areas.

Students then tackle Figure it Out (Sharan's house), section 6.2 p.147 ("Using Sharan's house floor plan (42 ft wide), find missing room dimensions and total area; compare areas and perimeters of both houses."). After finding Sharan's total area, they compare it with Charan's and also compare the perimeters of the two overall plans.
Discussion: can two house plans with different total areas have the same overall perimeter? Students reason and share examples.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes add all given dimensions instead of recovering missing ones first — insist they mark up the floor plan and check that their sub-dimensions sum to the given total in each direction. Comparing the two houses reinforces that area and perimeter are independent measures.
materials: Photocopied or drawn floor plan sheets for Charan's and Sharan's houses

periods.activity_title: Area Maze Puzzles — Multi-Step Reasoning with Sub-Rectangle Areas

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qa, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given sub-rectangle areas 13, 26, and 15 sq cm in a 2×2 grid arrangement, find the missing fourth area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qb, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given two sub-rectangles of 10 sq cm each with dimensions 2 cm and 3 cm visible, find the missing area of the third sub-rectangle (3 cm × 2 cm top right).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qc, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given a composite figure with total height 15 cm, sub-rectangles of 42 sq cm and 60 sq cm with some dimensions given, find the missing top sub-rectangle area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qd, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given two stacked sub-rectangles with areas 38 sq cm and 18 sq cm and dimensions 4 cm and 5 cm visible, find the missing width (top side length) of the larger rectangle.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the area-maze format: a rectangle divided into sub-rectangles; some areas and some dimensions are given; students must find the missing area or dimension. Model the key strategy on the board: if you know area and one side of a sub-rectangle, you can find the other side, and that side may be shared with a neighbour.

Students attempt Area Maze Puzzles Qa, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given sub-rectangle areas 13, 26, and 15 sq cm....") and Area Maze Puzzles Qb, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given two sub-rectangles of 10 sq cm each...."). They work individually first, then compare strategies with a partner.

Students tackle the harder puzzles: Area Maze Puzzles Qc, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given a composite figure with total height 15 cm, sub-rectangles of 42 sq cm and 60 sq cm....") and Area Maze Puzzles Qd, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given two stacked sub-rectangles with areas 38 sq cm and 18 sq cm...."). They annotate each step, labelling the side they deduced at each move.
Class share-out: students explain their chain of deductions for puzzle d. Highlight that these puzzles require no new formula — only the relationship area = length × breadth applied in reverse.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often try to guess missing dimensions rather than computing them from the given areas — stress that every deduction must be justified by a known area and a known side. Area maze puzzles reward systematic annotation: encourage students to write the deduced dimension directly on the figure.
materials: Printed or drawn area-maze puzzle sheets

periods.activity_title: Cutting a Rectangle to Discover the Triangle Area Formula

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Cut rectangle activity, section 6.3 p.142
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a rectangle, draw one diagonal, cut along the diagonal to produce two triangles; check whether the triangles overlap exactly and have the same area. Repeat with rectangles of different dimensions and with a square. Use grid paper to verify the triangle-rectangle area relationship for both right triangles and non-right triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.143
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the grid, find the area of blue triangle BAD in rectangle ABCD.

time_bands.activity: Students draw a rectangle on paper and mark its diagonal. Ask: 'If I cut along this diagonal, do the two pieces look the same? Do they have the same area?' Students predict and reason before cutting.

Students carry out Cut rectangle activity, section 6.3 p.142 ("Draw a rectangle, draw one diagonal, cut along the diagonal...."). They flip and superimpose the two triangles to confirm they are congruent. They then repeat with a different-sized rectangle and with a square, recording the rectangle's area and inferring that each triangle's area equals half the rectangle's.

Students use grid paper to verify the result numerically: they count the triangle's area on the grid (using partial-square conventions) and check it equals half the rectangle area. Then they attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.143 ("Using the grid, find the area of blue triangle BAD in rectangle ABCD."), applying the half-rectangle reasoning directly.

Teacher formalises: area of triangle = ½ × base × height, where base and height are the two sides of the enclosing rectangle. Students write the formula and note that it applies to right triangles at this stage; the next step extends it.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes cut unevenly and find the triangles do not match — suggest drawing the diagonal with a ruler before cutting. Establish clearly that the 'height' of the triangle in this context is the perpendicular side of the rectangle, not a slant side.
materials: Rectangular paper strips (at least two per student, different sizes)

periods.activity_title: Non-Right Triangles — Decomposing ABE to Extend the Formula

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.143
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the grid, find the area of red triangle ABE by decomposing into triangles AEF and BEF over sub-rectangles AFED and BFEC.

time_bands.activity: Draw rectangle ABCD on the board and mark a point E on side CD (not at a corner). Draw triangle ABE. Ask: 'Is ABE's area still half the rectangle? The apex is not above a base vertex — does the formula still hold?' Students discuss.

Develop the deductive argument: drop a perpendicular from E to AB, meeting AB at F. This splits rectangle ABCD into two sub-rectangles AFED and BFEC, and splits triangle ABE into two right triangles AEF and BEF. Since each right triangle is half its sub-rectangle, the total area of ABE = ½ × AFED + ½ × BFEC = ½ × (AFED + BFEC) = ½ × ABCD. Teacher writes each step, inviting students to supply the justification at each line.

Students verify the argument numerically using Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.143 ("Using the grid, find the area of red triangle ABE by decomposing into triangles AEF and BEF...."), counting grid squares for each sub-region and confirming the totals agree with the formula.

State the general principle: for any triangle with base b and corresponding perpendicular height h, area = ½ × b × h. Students copy the formula and note its derivation rests on the rectangle decomposition argument just made.

periods.teacher_notes: The key deductive step — splitting the non-right triangle into two right triangles each equal to half a sub-rectangle — is the logical core of this unit; take time at each step and ask students to state what property justifies it. Watch for students who try to apply ½ × b × h using a slant side instead of the perpendicular height.
materials: Whiteboard with a labelled diagram of ABCD and E

periods.activity_title: Composite Grid Figures — Splitting into Rectangles and Triangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure a on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure b on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure c on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1d, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure d on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1e, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure e on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

time_bands.activity: Review the two tools available: area of rectangle = l × b; area of triangle = ½ × b × h. Ask students how they would find the area of an irregular polygon on a grid. Establish the composite-decomposition strategy: split the figure into recognisable sub-shapes, find each area, and sum.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure a on the grid...."), Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure b...."), and Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure c...."). For each, they draw their splitting lines first, label base and height of every triangle, and compute sub-areas before summing.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1d, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure d....") and Figure it Out Q1e, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure e...."), which are more complex composites. Pairs compare splits and verify that different decompositions give the same total.
Quick debrief: which composite figure was hardest to split, and why? Reinforce that any split that covers the region exactly without gaps or overlaps is valid.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes use a slant side as the height of a triangle — prompt them to identify the base first and then find the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to that base. Encourage at least one alternative decomposition per figure to build flexibility.
materials: Grid paper with composite figures (printed or student-drawn)

periods.activity_title: Perimeter–Area Tension — Designing Shapes with Fixed Area but Different Perimeters

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q1, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using 9 connected unit squares, find the smallest possible perimeter.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q2, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using 9 connected unit squares, find the largest possible perimeter.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q3, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using 9 connected unit squares, make a figure with a perimeter of 18 units.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q4, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine whether other shaped figures can be made with the same perimeters found in Q1–Q3, or whether only one shape gives each perimeter; explain the reasoning.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw Shape A (area 18 sq units) and Shape B (area 20 sq units) such that Shape A has a longer perimeter than Shape B.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the central insight: area and perimeter are independent — the same area can pair with many different perimeters. Ask students to predict whether a shape with a larger area must always have a larger perimeter. Students discuss and give examples.

Students work through Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q1, section 6.3 p.145 ("Using 9 connected unit squares, find the smallest possible perimeter."), Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q2, section 6.3 p.145 ("Find the largest possible perimeter."), and Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q3, section 6.3 p.145 ("Make a figure with perimeter of 18 units.") on grid paper, exploring systematically.

Students address Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q4, section 6.3 p.145 ("Determine whether other shaped figures can be made with the same perimeters....") and then design responses to Figure it Out Q5, section 6.3 p.149 ("Draw Shape A (area 18 sq units) and Shape B (area 20 sq units) such that Shape A has a longer perimeter...."), explicitly constructing a counterexample to the 'bigger area = bigger perimeter' assumption.

Students share their Shape A and Shape B designs. The class verifies that each design satisfies the constraint. Articulate the lesson: area and perimeter are independent quantities — knowing one tells you nothing definitive about the other.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who struggle to find a solution to Q5 can be prompted to start with a very elongated Shape A (large perimeter, modest area) and a compact Shape B (small perimeter, larger area). The independence of area and perimeter is one of the chapter's deepest ideas and worth making the centrepiece of the discussion.

periods.activity_title: Inverse Area Problems and Design Challenges

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give dimensions of a rectangle whose area equals the sum of the areas of a 5 m × 10 m rectangle and a 2 m × 7 m rectangle.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: A rectangular garden 50 m long has area 1000 sq m; find its width.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Floor 5 m × 4 m; square carpet of side 3 m laid on it; find the area not carpeted.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Four flower beds 2 m × 1 m at corners of a garden 15 m × 12 m; find available lawn area.

time_bands.activity: Open with Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.149 ("Give dimensions of a rectangle whose area equals the sum of the areas of a 5 m × 10 m rectangle and a 2 m × 7 m rectangle."). Students first compute the target area (50 + 14 = 64 sq m) and then propose multiple valid rectangles — there are many factor pairs. Establish that the problem is open-ended.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.149 ("A rectangular garden 50 m long has area 1000 sq m; find its width.") and Figure it Out Q3, section 6.3 p.149 ("Floor 5 m × 4 m; square carpet of side 3 m...."). These are inverse and composite-subtraction problems respectively, applying area reasoning backwards and in combination.

Students solve Figure it Out Q4, section 6.3 p.149 ("Four flower beds 2 m × 1 m at corners of a garden 15 m × 12 m...."). They compute the total area of the four flower beds (4 × 2 = 8 sq m) and subtract from the garden area (180 – 8 = 172 sq m). Pairs check each other's working.

Quick oral round: teacher calls out a total area and one dimension; students call out the missing dimension. Close by noting that inverse problems — working backwards from area to dimension — appear in real contexts such as land use planning.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes forget to multiply the number of flower beds and subtract only one — prompt them to re-read the problem and mark all four corners before computing. Q1's open-endedness (many valid rectangles) can reassure students that a correct answer need not be unique.

periods.activity_title: Design Problems — Borders, Inner Rectangles and the Folded-Square Reasoning

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a rectangular border on a page that is 1 cm from top and bottom and 1.5 cm from left and right sides; find its perimeter.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a 12 units × 8 units rectangle; inside it draw another rectangle (not touching the outer) that occupies exactly half the area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: A square is folded in half and cut into two rectangles; identify which of four statements (a–d) about area and perimeter relationships is always true.

time_bands.activity: Students draw a rectangular border on their own page using a standard A4 sheet, measuring 1 cm from top and bottom and 1.5 cm from left and right — Figure it Out Q6, section 6.3 p.149 ("Draw a rectangular border on a page that is 1 cm from top and bottom and 1.5 cm from left and right...."). They then measure the border rectangle's dimensions and compute its perimeter.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q7, section 6.3 p.149 ("Draw a 12 units × 8 units rectangle; inside it draw another rectangle...that occupies exactly half the area."). The outer rectangle has area 96 sq units; the inner must have area 48 sq units. Students list factor pairs of 48 and draw an inner rectangle with one such pair of dimensions, verifying it fits inside the outer without touching the boundary.

Students reason through Figure it Out Q8, section 6.3 p.149 ("A square is folded in half and cut into two rectangles; identify which of four statements (a–d)...is always true."). They test each statement by computing areas and perimeters for a concrete square of known side length, then check whether the statement is always true or only sometimes true.

Class share-out for Q8: which statement is always true, and why? Students articulate the invariant — the total area is conserved but the perimeters of the two halves are each larger than half the original perimeter.

periods.teacher_notes: For Q7, students who pick a factor pair that is too large will find the inner rectangle does not fit — encourage them to check both dimensions fit strictly inside the outer boundary. The folded-square problem in Q8 rewards students who test a specific case first and then reason about whether the result generalises.

periods.activity_title: Mixed-Application Practice — Connecting All Area and Perimeter Techniques

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure a on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure b on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.3 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of composite figure c on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles.

time_bands.activity: Students revisit the three formulas: perimeter of a polygon (sum of sides), area of a rectangle (l × b), area of a triangle (½ × b × h). Teacher poses a quick-fire oral review — naming a shape and asking for the formula — to check fluency before a consolidation session.

Students rework Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure a on the grid by dividing into rectangles and triangles."), Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure b...."), and Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure c....") with a focus on accurate decomposition and clear labelling. Students who have not yet attempted these figures try them independently; those who have may rework them with a different decomposition to confirm the area is invariant.

Students pair up and pose each other an original composite-figure problem on grid paper — they draw a shape, compute its area themselves, then exchange papers and solve their partner's figure. Partners compare answers and resolve any discrepancies.
Brief close: students write one sentence about the most useful technique they practiced — decomposition, composite subtraction, or the triangle formula — and why it was useful.

periods.teacher_notes: This consolidation unit revisits the decomposition exercises as a capstone to the composite-figure strand; the student-posed problem in the final band makes a useful self-check of whether students can construct as well as solve. Watch for students who revert to perimeter formulas when asked for area — a confusion that suggests the boundary-vs-region distinction still needs reinforcing.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis — Connecting Perimeter, Area and the Triangle Formula

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give dimensions of a rectangle whose area equals the sum of the areas of a 5 m × 10 m rectangle and a 2 m × 7 m rectangle.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: A square is folded in half and cut into two rectangles; identify which of four statements (a–d) about area and perimeter relationships is always true.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 6.3 p.149
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw Shape A (area 18 sq units) and Shape B (area 20 sq units) such that Shape A has a longer perimeter than Shape B.

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-chapter concept map built live on the board: the teacher writes 'boundary' and 'region', and students contribute connections — perimeter formulas, area formulas, composite-subtraction technique, triangle decomposition, the independence of area and perimeter. Every term placed comes from a student, not from the teacher.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.149 ("Give dimensions of a rectangle whose area equals the sum of the areas of a 5 m × 10 m rectangle and a 2 m × 7 m rectangle."). They first compute the target area, then list multiple valid dimension pairs, computing the perimeter of each to observe that same-area rectangles have different perimeters — connecting the section 6.1 area-perimeter independence insight with section 6.2 area formulas.

Students engage with Figure it Out Q5, section 6.3 p.149 ("Draw Shape A (area 18 sq units) and Shape B (area 20 sq units) such that Shape A has a longer perimeter than Shape B.") and Figure it Out Q8, section 6.3 p.149 ("A square is folded in half and cut into two rectangles; identify which of four statements (a–d)...is always true."). These two items together draw on perimeter reasoning (section 6.1), area formulas (section 6.2), and the composite-shape argument (section 6.3).

Students write a three-sentence synthesis: what is perimeter, what is area, and how the area of any triangle relates to the enclosing rectangle — in their own words, without looking at their notes. Volunteers share; the class refines each statement together, arriving at precise, student-authored definitions to close the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The concept map in the opening band works best if the teacher resists filling in connections and waits for students to supply them — the productive silence is part of the synthesis. The final writing task surfaces lingering confusions between boundary and region and between base and height in the triangle formula; use it diagnostically.

items.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 18 cm and a breadth of 3 cm. What is its length?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 cm. Using P = 2 × (l + b): 18 = 2 × (l + 3), so l + 3 = 9, giving l = 6 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Substitute into P = 2 × (l + b) and solve for the unknown length.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student subtracted only breadth from perimeter (18 − 3 = 15) without dividing by 2, omitting the factor of 2 in the formula.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student halved the perimeter (18 ÷ 2 = 9) but then subtracted breadth from 9 incorrectly as 9 − 3 = 6 — wait, this gives 6; the student who chooses 12 likely added breadth instead: 9 + 3 = 12.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly computed half the perimeter (9) but did not subtract the breadth, treating 9 as the length.

inclusivity.support: Look back at the rectangle perimeter formula in section 6.1 to recall that opposite sides are equal.
inclusivity.challenge: State a second pair of dimensions that also gives a perimeter of 18 cm and explain why infinitely many such rectangles exist.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132
exercise.description: Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm and breadth is 2 cm.

items.prompt: A piece of wire is bent into a rectangle of length 8 cm and breadth 5 cm. The same wire is straightened and bent into a square. What is the side length of the square?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6.5 cm. Wire length = perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm. Side of square = 26 ÷ 4 = 6.5 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the rectangle's perimeter (the fixed wire length) and divide by 4 to find the square's side.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student found l + b = 13 and used that as the side, forgetting to multiply by 2 to get the total wire length first.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student used the breadth of the rectangle as the side of the square, not using the perimeter at all.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly found the perimeter 26 cm but stopped there, using the total perimeter as the side length without dividing by 4.

inclusivity.support: Re-read the wire problem in section 6.1 and notice that the wire length stays constant — it equals the rectangle's perimeter.
inclusivity.challenge: If the same wire were bent into an equilateral triangle instead, what would each side measure? Justify your answer.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.132
exercise.description: A wire bent into a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle is straightened and re-bent into a square; find the side length of the square.

items.prompt: A rectangular hall is 20 m long and has an area of 300 sq m. What is its breadth?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15 m. Area = l × b, so b = Area ÷ l = 300 ÷ 20 = 15 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rearrange the area formula b = Area ÷ l and divide.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student subtracted the length from the area (300 − 20 = 280) instead of dividing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplied area by length (300 × 20 = 6000), confusing inverse operation with the forward formula.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student halved the length (20 ÷ 2 = 10), applying a perimeter-style operation rather than the area relationship.

inclusivity.support: Write the area formula as a multiplication sentence and cover one factor to find the missing one.
inclusivity.challenge: Find all whole-number dimensions a rectangle could have if its area is 300 sq m, and state which gives the smallest perimeter.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.138
exercise.description: A rectangular garden 25 m long has area 300 sq m; find the width.

items.prompt: A rectangular field is 80 m long and 60 m wide. Each tree in the field needs 40 sq m of space. What is the maximum number of trees that can be planted?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 120. Field area = 80 × 60 = 4800 sq m. Number of trees = 4800 ÷ 40 = 120.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the field's area using Area = l × b, then divide by the area needed per tree.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added all given numbers (80 + 60 + 40 + 100 = 280 or similar), not applying area reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student divided only one dimension by the per-tree area (60 ÷ not 40, or confused the breadth with the count), likely using the breadth 60 directly as the answer.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student computed the field area (4800) and stopped, not dividing by the per-tree requirement.

inclusivity.support: First find the total area of the field; then think of dividing that area into equal 40 sq m plots.
inclusivity.challenge: If the per-tree space requirement increases to 50 sq m, how many fewer trees fit? Explain why the answer is not simply 4800 ÷ 50 − 4800 ÷ 40 in absolute terms.

exercise.description: A coconut grove 100 m × 50 m; each tree needs 25 sq m; find the maximum number of trees.

items.prompt: Rectangle PQRS has length 10 cm and breadth 6 cm. A diagonal PR divides the rectangle into two triangles. Explain, using the relationship between the rectangle and the triangles, why triangle PQR must have an area of exactly 30 sq cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two triangles formed by diagonal PR — triangle PQR and triangle PSR — are congruent (they are mirror images that fit exactly over each other). Together they make up the full rectangle, whose area is 10 × 6 = 60 sq cm. Since the two congruent triangles share the total area equally, each triangle has area 60 ÷ 2 = 30 sq cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The diagonal splits the rectangle into two congruent halves, so each triangle's area equals half the rectangle's area.

inclusivity.support: Try explaining your thinking to a partner before writing — say how many triangles the diagonal makes and whether they look the same.
inclusivity.challenge: What if PR were not a diagonal but connected P to a point M on QR that is 4 cm from Q — would triangle PQM still be half the rectangle? Explain.

items.prompt: Rectangle ABCD has length 12 cm and breadth 8 cm. Point E lies on side CD so that DE = 4 cm and EC = 8 cm. Triangle ABE is drawn. A student claims: 'I can find the area of triangle ABE by splitting it into two right triangles — one for each part of the rectangle.' Show the student's reasoning step by step, and state the area of triangle ABE.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Drop a perpendicular from E to AB, meeting AB at F where AF = DE = 4 cm and FB = EC = 8 cm. This splits rectangle ABCD into sub-rectangle AFED (4 cm × 8 cm, area 32 sq cm) and sub-rectangle FBCE (8 cm × 8 cm, area 64 sq cm). Triangle AEF is half of AFED, so its area = 16 sq cm. Triangle BEF is half of FBCE, so its area = 32 sq cm. Total area of triangle ABE = 16 + 32 = 48 sq cm. Equivalently, ½ × 12 × 8 = 48 sq cm, confirming the result equals half the full rectangle's area.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Drop a perpendicular from E to the base AB to create two sub-rectangles; each right triangle is half its sub-rectangle, and the sum equals half the full rectangle's area.

inclusivity.support: Draw the perpendicular from E to AB on your diagram first; label each new smaller rectangle and find its area before moving on.
inclusivity.challenge: Would the area of triangle ABE change if E moved to a different point on CD — say DE = 6 cm? Reason without computing a new value.

items.prompt: A rectangular running track is 80 m long and 50 m wide. Priya runs 5 complete rounds of the track. What total distance does Priya cover? If Rohit runs the same total distance on a square track, what is the side length of that square track?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Perimeter of rectangular track = 2 × (80 + 50) = 260 m. Total distance for 5 rounds = 5 × 260 = 1300 m. For the square track: side = 1300 ÷ 4 = 325 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the rectangle's perimeter, multiply by the number of rounds, then divide by 4 for the square's side.

inclusivity.support: Draw the rectangular track, label the sides, and compute the perimeter of one round before multiplying by 5.
inclusivity.challenge: If Rohit instead ran on an equilateral triangular track covering the same 1300 m, what would each side measure? Compare the two tracks' sides and explain which track has more turns per side.

items.prompt: A dot-grid figure has a boundary made of 5 straight segments (each 1 unit long) and 3 diagonal segments (each longer than 1 unit). Can you say, with only this information, that the perimeter of the figure is 8 units? Explain why or why not.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. The perimeter cannot be stated as 8 units. The 5 straight segments contribute 5 units, but each diagonal segment is longer than 1 unit — a diagonal on a dot grid connects two dots at the corners of a unit square, so its length is √2 ≈ 1.41 units, not 1 unit. The perimeter is 5 + 3√2 units (approximately 9.24 units), not 8 units. Straight and diagonal segments must be counted separately and cannot be added as if equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that diagonal segments on a dot grid are longer than straight segments and express the perimeter in terms of straight (s) and diagonal (d) units.

inclusivity.support: Look at a dot-grid square: the side going straight across is 1 unit; the corner-to-corner diagonal looks longer — try measuring both with a ruler.
inclusivity.challenge: If a dot-grid triangle has all three sides as diagonals, express its perimeter in terms of d and explain why that perimeter is more than 3 units.

items.prompt: A 10 cm × 4 cm rectangle is cut into two equal halves along its length to produce two 10 cm × 2 cm pieces. The two pieces are rejoined so that the 2 cm edges are placed side by side (making an L-shape). What is the perimeter of the resulting figure?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When the two 10 cm × 2 cm pieces are placed side by side along their 2 cm edges, the joined edge (2 cm) is shared and hidden on each piece. Outer boundary: the outer boundary of the L-shape has sides of 10, 2, 8, 2, 2, and 4 cm — checking: starting from the top-left corner of the L and going clockwise: 10 (top), 2 (right of top piece going down), 8 (going left — the 10 cm bottom of top piece minus the 2 cm covered by the join), wait — let us recount carefully. The two pieces form an L. Piece 1 horizontal, Piece 2 perpendicular at one end. Perimeter = 10 + 2 + 8 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 28 cm. Verification: original rectangle perimeter = 2 × (10 + 4) = 28 cm; joining along a 2 cm edge removes 2 × 2 = 4 cm and the new L-shape exposes the same lengths, so perimeter = 28 cm. Both routes confirm 28 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the outer boundary of the L-shape, noting that each shared edge is hidden and its length is removed twice from the total.

inclusivity.support: Cut and physically join two strips of paper as described, then trace the outer edge with your finger and measure each side.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a different way to join the two 10 cm × 2 cm pieces so that the resulting perimeter is as small as possible, and justify your answer.

items.prompt: Nine unit squares are arranged in a connected figure. One student says the smallest possible perimeter is 12 units and the largest is 20 units. Another student says you can also make a figure with perimeter 14 units using 9 squares. Who is right and who is wrong? Justify your answers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both students are right. The compact 3 × 3 square arrangement gives the smallest perimeter of 12 units. The linear 1 × 9 strip gives the largest perimeter of 20 units. A figure with perimeter 14 units is also achievable — for example, a 3 × 3 square with one corner square detached and reattached on an outer side in a less compact configuration, giving perimeter between 12 and 20. Not all even values in this range are achievable, but 14 is, so the second student is also correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason about how many sides become shared when squares are connected — compact arrangements maximise shared sides and minimise perimeter; linear arrangements minimise shared sides and maximise perimeter.

inclusivity.support: Draw a 3 × 3 square on grid paper and count the boundary squares by tracing the outer edge; then stretch the same squares into a row and count again.
inclusivity.challenge: List all even perimeter values between 12 and 20 and determine which ones are achievable with 9 connected unit squares, justifying each case.

items.prompt: Two tangram pieces look different in shape but a student claims they have the same area. Without measuring, how could the student use the tangram pieces to check this claim? Describe the method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student can place one tangram piece on top of the other to see if they cover exactly the same amount of space (superposition). Alternatively, if both pieces can each be assembled from the same number of copies of the smallest tangram piece (Shape C), their areas are equal — since each copy of Shape C has the same area. Equal area does not require equal shape, so the pieces may look different yet tile the same region.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Superpose the pieces or express each as a multiple of the smallest piece to compare areas without measuring.

inclusivity.support: Try physically placing one tangram piece on another and see whether one fits exactly inside the other or sticks out.
inclusivity.challenge: Two pieces have the same area but different perimeters — draw a sketch of two such shapes and measure each perimeter to confirm they differ.

items.prompt: Seven tangram pieces are rearranged into a rectangle. The smallest tangram piece has area 2 sq cm. What is the area of the rectangle? How does its perimeter compare to the square made from the same seven pieces?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The seven tangram pieces always have the same total area regardless of arrangement. If the smallest piece (Shape C) has area 2 sq cm, the full tangram square has area 8 × 2 = 16 sq cm (since all 7 pieces together equal 8 units of Shape C). The rectangle formed from the same pieces also has area 16 sq cm — area is conserved. However, the perimeter of the rectangle differs from the perimeter of the square: a square of area 16 sq cm has side 4 cm and perimeter 16 cm, while a rectangle with the same area but different dimensions (e.g., 2 cm × 8 cm) has perimeter 20 cm. So the areas are equal but the perimeters are generally different.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Total area is the sum of all pieces (8 × area of Shape C); rearrangement preserves area but changes perimeter.

inclusivity.support: Count how many times the smallest tangram piece fits into the full square, then use that count for the rectangle too.
inclusivity.challenge: If the seven pieces are arranged into a rectangle whose shorter side is 2 cm, what are the dimensions and perimeter of that rectangle? Show your working.

items.prompt: A rectangular school courtyard is 18 m long and 12 m wide. A 2 m wide corridor runs along the inside of all four walls. What is the area of the floor space outside the corridor (i.e., the corridor strip itself)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Area of the full courtyard = 18 × 12 = 216 sq m. The inner open space (inside all four corridor strips) has dimensions (18 − 2 − 2) × (12 − 2 − 2) = 14 × 8 = 112 sq m. Area of corridor = 216 − 112 = 104 sq m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the inner rectangle's area from the outer rectangle's area to find the corridor strip area.

inclusivity.support: Draw the courtyard as a large rectangle and shade the corridor band; then draw the inner unshaded rectangle and compute both areas before subtracting.
inclusivity.challenge: If the corridor width is changed to 3 m, what is the new corridor area? Explain in one sentence how the corridor area changes as the width increases.

items.prompt: A house has an overall floor plan that is 24 ft wide and 30 ft long. Inside, one room is 12 ft wide and 15 ft long, and another is 12 ft wide and 10 ft long. Both rooms share the 24 ft width. Find the area of the remaining part of the house (everything except those two rooms).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total house area = 24 × 30 = 720 sq ft. Area of room 1 = 12 × 15 = 180 sq ft. Area of room 2 = 12 × 10 = 120 sq ft. Remaining area = 720 − 180 − 120 = 420 sq ft.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the total area and subtract the areas of both rooms.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the floor plan and label each room's dimensions before computing any areas.
inclusivity.challenge: If the remaining 420 sq ft is divided into two equal rectangular spaces, what are the possible whole-number dimensions for each space?

items.prompt: A large rectangle is divided into four smaller rectangles. Three of the sub-rectangles have areas 18 sq cm, 24 sq cm, and 12 sq cm. The width of the left column of sub-rectangles is 3 cm and the height of the top row is 4 cm. Find the area of the fourth sub-rectangle.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Sub-rect top-left (18 sq cm) | Sub-rect top-right (?) |
| Sub-rect bottom-left (12 sq cm) | Sub-rect bottom-right (24 sq cm) |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Left column width = 3 cm. Top-left area = 18 sq cm = 3 × h_top, so h_top = 6 cm. Bottom-left area = 12 sq cm = 3 × h_bottom, so h_bottom = 4 cm. Right column width: top-right area — we need the right column width. Top-right is in the same row as top-left (height 6 cm). Top-right area / 6 = right-column width. Bottom-right area = 24 sq cm; height = 4 cm, so right-column width = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm. Top-right area = 6 cm × 6 cm = 36 sq cm. Verification: 18 + 36 + 12 + 24 = 90 sq cm. Large rectangle = (3 + 6) × (6 + 4) = 9 × 10 = 90 sq cm. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use known areas and one side to find shared dimensions; each shared dimension feeds the adjacent sub-rectangle.

inclusivity.support: Start with the sub-rectangle whose area and one side you know; compute the missing side and check whether that side is shared with the unknown sub-rectangle.
inclusivity.challenge: Swap the positions of the 18 sq cm and 12 sq cm sub-rectangles and recompute the missing area — does it change? Explain why.

items.prompt: On a grid, a composite figure is made of a 6-unit × 4-unit rectangle with a triangle attached on one of the 6-unit sides. The triangle has a base of 6 units and a height of 3 units. Find the total area of the composite figure.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Area of rectangle = 6 × 4 = 24 sq units. Area of triangle = ½ × 6 × 3 = 9 sq units. Total area = 24 + 9 = 33 sq units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute rectangle area using l × b and triangle area using ½ × b × h, then add both.

items.prompt: Nine connected unit squares are arranged in two different configurations. Configuration P is a 3 × 3 square, and Configuration Q is a 1 × 9 strip. Both have the same area. A student says Configuration Q must have a bigger perimeter because it is more spread out. Is the student's reasoning correct? Compute both perimeters to confirm your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student's reasoning is correct. Configuration P (3 × 3 square): perimeter = 4 × 3 = 12 units. Configuration Q (1 × 9 strip): perimeter = 2 × (9 + 1) = 20 units. Both have area 9 sq units, but Q's perimeter (20 units) is greater than P's (12 units). Spreading the same area into a longer shape increases the perimeter because fewer sides are shared between adjacent squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute each perimeter using P = 2 × (l + b) for the rectangle, confirming that greater elongation gives greater perimeter for the same area.

inclusivity.support: Draw both configurations on grid paper and trace the outer boundary with a pencil, counting the unit edges as you go.

items.prompt: Find three different pairs of whole-number dimensions for a rectangle whose area equals the combined area of a 6 m × 9 m rectangle and a 4 m × 6 m rectangle. State the perimeter of each of your three rectangles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Combined area = 6 × 9 + 4 × 6 = 54 + 24 = 78 sq m. Factor pairs of 78: 1 × 78, 2 × 39, 3 × 26, 6 × 13. Three valid rectangles (any three): (1) 2 m × 39 m, perimeter = 2 × (2 + 39) = 82 m. (2) 3 m × 26 m, perimeter = 2 × (3 + 26) = 58 m. (3) 6 m × 13 m, perimeter = 2 × (6 + 13) = 38 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the target area as the sum of the two given areas, then list factor pairs and apply P = 2 × (l + b) for each.

inclusivity.support: First add the two areas to find the target, then list pairs of numbers that multiply to give that target.
inclusivity.challenge: Among all whole-number dimension rectangles with this area, identify which has the smallest perimeter and explain why it is close to a square.

items.prompt: Shape A is drawn on grid paper with area 18 sq units. Shape B is drawn with area 24 sq units. A student draws Shape A as a very thin 1 × 18 rectangle and Shape B as a compact 4 × 6 rectangle. Compute the perimeter of each shape and check whether Shape A really does have a longer perimeter than Shape B in this case.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape A (1 × 18 rectangle): perimeter = 2 × (1 + 18) = 38 units. Shape B (4 × 6 rectangle): perimeter = 2 × (4 + 6) = 20 units. Shape A (area 18) has a longer perimeter (38 units) than Shape B (area 24, perimeter 20 units). So yes, the shape with the smaller area has the longer perimeter in this case — confirming that area and perimeter are independent.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply P = 2 × (l + b) to each rectangle and compare; an elongated shape with smaller area can have a larger perimeter than a compact shape with larger area.

inclusivity.support: Draw both rectangles on grid paper, trace the outer boundary, and count the unit edges to verify the perimeter.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a pair of shapes where the one with the larger area also has the larger perimeter, and a different pair where the one with the larger area has the smaller perimeter.

items.prompt: A notebook page measures 28 cm long and 22 cm wide. A rectangular border is drawn 2 cm from the top and bottom edges and 2.5 cm from the left and right edges. What is the perimeter of the border rectangle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Border rectangle length = 28 − 2 − 2 = 24 cm. Border rectangle width = 22 − 2.5 − 2.5 = 17 cm. Perimeter = 2 × (24 + 17) = 2 × 41 = 82 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the two margin widths from each dimension and apply P = 2 × (l + b).

inclusivity.support: Draw the page, mark the margins on all four sides, and measure what remains before computing the perimeter.
inclusivity.challenge: If the border is moved 1 cm further from each edge (3 cm top/bottom, 3.5 cm left/right), by how much does the perimeter decrease?

items.prompt: A square piece of paper has side 10 cm. It is folded exactly in half and then cut along the fold, producing two identical rectangles. For one of those rectangles, state its area and perimeter. Then explain whether the perimeter of the rectangle is more than, less than, or equal to half the perimeter of the original square.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Original square: side = 10 cm, area = 100 sq cm, perimeter = 40 cm. One rectangle (from folding in half along the length): dimensions 10 cm × 5 cm. Area = 50 sq cm (half the square's area). Perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (10 + 5) = 30 cm. Half the square's perimeter = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm. The rectangle's perimeter (30 cm) is greater than half the square's perimeter (20 cm). The cut creates two new edges (5 cm each, one per rectangle), so each rectangle gains an extra side compared to half the original boundary.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the rectangle's dimensions from the fold, then compare its perimeter to half the square's perimeter to see the effect of the new cut edge.

inclusivity.support: Fold and cut a square piece of paper and measure the resulting rectangle's sides to check your answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Would the perimeter relationship change if the fold were along the other axis? Compute and compare for a non-square rectangle to generalise.
